orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, going on with her story to Lockwood after their late-night chat. She begins in June 1778, the summer she mentioned at the end of Chapter VII. Partway through, she points out a portrait hanging in the room where they sit at the Grange.

notes.g: The first lovely baby I looked after.
notes.n: A 'nursling' is a baby in someone's care. 'Bonny' is the northern word for pretty or fine.

notes.t: the last of the ancient Earnshaw stock
notes.g: The last of the old Earnshaw family line.
notes.n: Remember the name 'Hareton Earnshaw' and the date 1500 carved over the door in Chapter I. The family has lived at the Heights for centuries.

notes.g: Making hay: cutting grass and drying it to feed animals in winter.
notes.n: June is haymaking time, and everyone on a farm helped, women included.

notes.g: A field of grass grown for hay.
The mistress (Frances) is going to die.
notes.n: 'Missis' is the dialect form of 'mistress'.

A lung disease and the great killer of the age. Its signs were a cough, breathlessness, weight loss, flushed cheeks and bright eyes. Look back at Frances's symptoms in Chapter VI. Emily Brontë's two eldest sisters died of it as children.

notes.g: Nothing left to hold her to life (now the baby is born).
You're to look after the baby.
notes.m: Nelly is a nanny, not a wet nurse: she will feed it 'with sugar and milk'.

notes.g: My hay rake, for turning and gathering cut grass.
A woman's hat, tied under the chin.
She looks well; she looks fine.

notes.t: out of her head for joy

notes.m: 'Fairly' here means completely. 'Mad' meaning angry was common in English dialect, not only American.

notes.g: Probably the local midwife, who delivered the baby.
notes.n: 'Dame' was a title for an older woman of the village.

notes.g: The gloomy old prophet of doom (the doctor).
notes.n: A 'croaker' is someone who always predicts disaster, like a croaking raven.

notes.g: A frail, skinny girl, as thin as a reed.
notes.n: A rush is a thin, grass-like plant that grows in wet ground.
Nelly's biblical word: an idol is a false god.

notes.g: Visiting and treating her as her doctor.
notes.n: Doctors charged for each visit, as Kenneth's word 'expense' shows.

notes.g: Hindley insists it was a passing fever, which people recovered from.
notes.n: Consumption was understood to be incurable.

notes.t: her pulse is as slow as mine now, and her cheek as cool
notes.g: Hindley claims the signs of fever have gone.
notes.n: A fast pulse and flushed cheeks were typical of consumption.
So the rough young man Lockwood met at the Heights in Chapters II and III is this baby, Hindley's son, as Nelly said in Chapter IV.

notes.t: his sorrow was of that kind that will not lament
notes.g: His grief was the kind that doesn't show itself in tears.
Wild, self-destructive living: heavy drinking and gambling.
Someone raised alongside him like a sister.
notes.n: Nelly's mother was Hindley's nurse (Chapter IV), so the two grew up together.

notes.g: Bully the tenant farmers and farm workers.
notes.n: 'Hector' comes from the Trojan hero Hector, whose name came to mean a blustering bully.
A religious word: a vocation is a calling from God. Nelly is being sarcastic about Joseph.

notes.g: A fine example (said ironically: a terrible one).
notes.m: 'Pretty' here is sarcastic and has nothing to do with looks.

notes.t: enough to make a fiend of a saint
notes.g: Enough to turn a saint into a devil.

notes.n: 'Redemption' is the religious word for being saved from sin.

notes.g: The most admired girl in the district.

notes.t: a wondrous constancy to old attachments
notes.g: A remarkable loyalty to old friends.

notes.n: In this chapter 'Linton' on its own means Edgar.

notes.g: Edgar Linton became Nelly's master here at the Grange, and is now dead.
notes.n: 'Late' means dead. So Edgar is the 'late master' of Chapter IV, whose daughter is young Mrs. Heathcliff.

notes.g: His wife's portrait used to hang on the other side.
notes.n: Lockwood's comment just below makes clear that the wife was Catherine Earnshaw.

notes.t: exceedingly resembling the young lady at the Heights
notes.g: Very like young Mrs. Heathcliff, whom Lockwood met at Wuthering Heights.
notes.n: No surprise: Chapter IV told us she is the late master's daughter.

notes.t: with a mind to correspond with his person
notes.g: If his mind matched his gentle looks.

notes.t: fancy my idea of Catherine Earnshaw
notes.g: Fall for the wild Catherine Earnshaw I have been picturing.

notes.n: 'Ingenious' usually means clever. It may be meant as 'ingenuous' (frank and natural), since Nelly says Catherine wasn't deliberately deceiving.

notes.m: 'Vulgar' meant common or lower-class, not crude or obscene.

notes.g: Edgar Linton, as the servants call him.
Knowing Edgar came to court Catherine.
notes.n: Hindley keeps out of the way rather than offend him, which suggests he is happy to see the richer Lintons courting his sister.

notes.g: Turn into someone to give her advice.

notes.t: presumed to give himself a holiday
notes.g: Took it upon himself to take a day off.

notes.t: that his present aspect retains no traces of
notes.g: Which his appearance today shows no sign of.
notes.n: Lockwood described the grown Heathcliff in Chapter I as looking like a gentleman.

notes.t: there was no prevailing on him

notes.g: Went downhill along with his mind.
notes.m: 'Sympathise' here means change in step with something, not feel pity.

notes.g: A silk dress: much too fine for a rainy afternoon at home.
notes.n: Heathcliff guesses at once that she is expecting a visitor.

notes.g: An hour after the midday meal.

notes.n: Lime, made by burning limestone, was spread on fields to improve sour moorland soil.

notes.g: A rocky outcrop on the moors near the Heights.

notes.t: smooth the way for an intrusion
notes.g: Prepare Heathcliff for an unwelcome visit.
Said they might pay a visit.

notes.n: Almanacs listed the days with saints' days, moon phases and weather lore. Heathcliff has been keeping score on it.

notes.g: You might as well be unable to speak.

notes.n: Coalfields lay not far from these moors. Nelly sets Heathcliff's grim looks against Edgar's gentle ones.

notes.t: pronounced his words as you do
notes.g: Spoke like an educated gentleman, as Lockwood does, not with the local accent.

notes.m: 'Plate' here means the household's silver or silver-plated dishes, not a single dinner plate.

notes.g: A kitchen sideboard with shelves above for dishes and drawers below.
Stay in the room as a chaperone.
notes.n: A respectable young lady was not supposed to be left alone with a young man.

notes.t: a decided purple witness to refute her
notes.g: A clear purple bruise to prove her wrong.
Catherine is Hareton's aunt: his father's sister.

notes.m: 'Livid' here means discoloured, bluish, not furious. 'Waxed' means grew.

notes.g: The connecting door between the rooms.
Eyelids to blink fast (holding back tears).

notes.n: In northern speech 'marred' means spoiled by indulgence.

notes.t: he’s doomed, and flies to his fate
notes.g: Nelly's dramatic thought: he can't escape, like a bird flying into a trap.

notes.n: 'Rabid' means mad, like a dog with rabies.

notes.m: 'Intimacy' meant close friendship, with no sexual meaning. 'Effected' means brought about.

notes.g: The outer defences of their shyness.
notes.n: A military image: outworks are the outer walls of a fortress.

notes.m: 'Lovers' meant sweethearts, a courting couple. No sexual meaning.

notes.g: News that Hindley had come home.
notes.m: 'Intelligence' here means news or information, not cleverness.

notes.g: The lead pellets loaded into the gun.
A light shotgun for shooting birds.
